title: De altitudine columnarum sub proprio pondere corruentium

deep.reconstruction:
Problem and method. The page belongs to Euler's 1778 attempt (E510) to find the height at which a vertical column buckles under its own weight. The governing linear ODE has a coefficient linear in the arc length, a heavy-column equation of Airy type. Its solutions are power series in a cubic variable. In modern terms they are Airy or Bessel-of-order-±1/3 functions, which Euler of course does not name. In §33 Euler wrote these as series P, P', Q, Q' in a parameter t. In §35–36 he evaluates them numerically for the trial value t = 200 (lt = log 200 = 2.3010300). The aim is presumably to test a boundary or critical condition built from these four sums.

Scheme of computation. All work is in 7-place common logarithms; characteristics such as 9 or 8 mean logarithm minus 10. Each step:
- adds log t;
- subtracts the log of a divisor D_m, giving log|term_m|;
- takes the antilog to 4 decimals with alternating signs;
- accumulates a running partial sum beneath each term.

Part 1: series P (continued from p.187). The steps on this page are:
- lXI = 9.3267751 gives XI = +0.2122.
- 9.3267751 + 2.3010300 - 3.0637814 = 8.5640237 gives XII = -0.0366.
- 0.8650537 - 3.1370931 = 7.7279606 gives XIII = +0.0053.
- 0.0289906 - 3.2047065 = 6.8242841 gives XIV = -0.0007.
- Partial sums: 0.2054, 0.1688, 0.1741, 0.1734. So P(200) ≈ 0.1734.

The divisors behave as follows:
- D_6 ≈ 258.43, D_7 ≈ 363.38, D_8 ≈ 486.32, D_9 ≈ 627.27, …, D_12 ≈ 1158.3, D_13 ≈ 1371, D_14 ≈ 1602.4.
- Their second differences are about 18, so D_m ≈ 9m² - 12m + 6.4 ≈ 3m(3m-4) + 6.4.
- In this range D_m is therefore not a simple rational product. It may come from coefficients that were themselves computed numerically; I did not identify §33's exact formula.

Part 2: series P'. Its terms are exactly P'_m = P_m/(3m-1):
- VI'/VI = 1/17, VII'/VII = 1/20, …, XI'/XI = 1/32.
- XII' = 0.036645/35 ≈ 0.0010 and XIII' = 0.005345/38 ≈ 0.0001.
- Partial sums: 0.1640, 0.1630, 0.1631. The next term (≈1.6·10⁻⁵) is rightly dropped.
- So P'(200) ≈ 0.1631.

Part 3: §36, series Q and Q'. The first terms are:
- Q_1 = t/6 = 33.3333, since 2.3010300 - log 6 = 1.5228787.
- Q_2 = -Q_1·t/40 = -166.6667, since 3.8259087 - log 40 = 2.2218487.

From the divisors on this and the next page (40, 84, 146.67, 227.5, 326.4, 443.3, 578.3) one recovers the exact recursion:
- Q_m/Q_{m-1} = -t(m-1)/[m(3m-1)(3m-2)].
- Hence m·Q_m = (-1)^{m-1} t^m / [3 ∏_{k≤m}(3k-1)(3k-2)].
- This is t^m/(3m) times the coefficients of an Airy-type series in u = x³, i.e. an integral of an Airy-type function.

Q' satisfies Q'_m = Q_m/(3m+1):
- I' = 33.3333/4 = 8.3333.
- II' = 166.6667/7 = 23.8095.

The partial sums I + II = -133.3334 and I' + II' = -15.4762 are carried to the next page.

The factors 1/(3m-1) and 1/(3m+1) show that P' and Q' are the series obtained by one more integration in the original variable x (t ∝ x³). The page is a routine numerical table: the sums show large alternating terms (up to ~500) cancelling to small values, handled adequately with 4 decimals.
errors:
No arithmetic errors found on this page.
- All log subtractions check: 1.6278051-3.0637814→8.5640237; 0.8650537-3.1370931→7.7279606; 0.0289906-3.2047065→6.8242841.
- All antilogs (0.21225, 0.036645, 0.005345, 0.000667) round correctly.
- All partial sums are correct.
- Q_1, Q_2, Q'_1, Q'_2 and their sums are correct.

Minor point: the Q-series terms are large and alternating (|terms| up to ~541 on the next page), so the 4-decimal sums lose relative accuracy. With 7-place logarithms the absolute error stays around 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻³, which is adequate for Euler's purpose.

Outside this page: Truesdell is often cited as judging Euler's overall treatment of the heavy column in these late papers flawed or inconclusive, with the correct critical height usually credited to Greenhill (1881). Unsure about the specifics; nothing on this page itself is wrong.

ideas.what: Numerical evaluation of the power-series solutions of the heavy-column buckling equation at a trial parameter value, using 7-place logarithms and running partial sums.
ideas.modern_name: Series evaluation of Airy/Bessel(±1/3) functions; numerical solution of the self-weight buckling eigenvalue problem
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (series, 1778); Greenhill 1881 (Bessel-function solution and critical height 7.837 EI/q)
ideas.where_published: E510 itself, Acta Academiae Scientiarum Petropolitanae 1778 (publ. 1780); related heavy-column papers of 1778 (E508, E509 — unsure of exact numbers)

ideas.what: Companion series obtained by dividing the m-th term by (3m-1) (for P') or (3m+1) (for Q'), i.e. termwise integration in the original variable x with t ∝ x³.
ideas.modern_name: Termwise integration of power series; integrals of Airy-type functions

ideas.what: Q-series with exact hypergeometric recursion Q_m/Q_{m-1} = -t(m-1)/[m(3m-1)(3m-2)].
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (this paper); later Gauss/Clausen general theory

deep.surprise_reason: This is a purely numerical page: the continuation of tables evaluating four series at t = 200, all arithmetic correct. The only content is the series structure, which is already stated in §33 of the published paper and covered in histories of the heavy-column problem (Truesdell). Nothing new or uncredited appears.
transcription_corrections:
The transcription matches the image.
- Characteristics 9, 8, 7, 6 in lXI…lXIV are logarithms minus 10, the standard tabular convention, not misreadings.
- The final 'lII =' at the bottom is a catchword for the next page.
